story.prologue.1: [Deniz — CEO]: Welcome. The bad news: Null, our only infrastructure engineer, quit on Friday.
story.prologue.2: [Deniz]: The good news: you're taking their place. The investor demo is 6 weeks out and the system is a house of cards.
story.prologue.3: [Nova — Senior Engineer]: Hey, I'm Nova. Don't panic — I'm not leaving you on your own.
story.prologue.4: [Nova]: This is a marathon. We start at the terminal and turn Meridian into a platform that actually stays up.
story.prologue.5: [Nova]: If you're ready, let's put out the first fire together. Type 'quests' to see your assignment.
story.acts.fundamentals.title: ACT I — Trial by Fire
story.acts.fundamentals.intro.0: [Nova]: Prod runs on a single server and the deploy is broken right now.
story.acts.fundamentals.intro.1: [Nova]: First you'll learn to stand on your own feet in the terminal — we'll type every command together.
story.acts.fundamentals.intro.2: [Nova]: By the end of the day you'll be speaking this place's language.
story.acts.fundamentals.outro.0: [Nova]: First week done and you're still standing. The terminal isn't your enemy anymore — it's your tool.
story.acts.fundamentals.outro.1: [Deniz]: Not bad, rookie. But the real work starts now: this single server is going to kill us. We're moving to the cloud.
story.acts.cloud-core.title: ACT II — Into the Cloud
story.acts.cloud-core.intro.0: [Deniz]: We can't walk into an investor demo on one rented server. We're going to AWS.
story.acts.cloud-core.intro.1: [Nova]: We'll build a solid cloud foundation from scratch: identity, network, compute, storage, database. In order.
story.acts.cloud-core.outro.0: [Nova]: Meridian is on a real cloud now. The demo server won't fall over.
story.acts.cloud-core.outro.1: [Deniz]: Good. But last night I changed one setting by hand and we were down for 20 minutes. That will not happen again.
story.acts.iac.title: ACT III — Never By Hand Again
story.acts.iac.intro.0: [Nova]: Yesterday's outage came from a hand-made change. The fix: put the infrastructure into code.
story.acts.iac.intro.1: [Nova]: We'll build it with Terraform so that if everything is wiped, one command brings it all back.
story.acts.iac.outro.0: [Nova]: Our infrastructure is code now. Nobody can break something permanent by accident.
story.acts.iac.outro.1: [Deniz]: The demo was perfect — the funding came through! But user count exploded and the system is barely holding.
story.acts.containers.title: ACT IV — The Scale Test
story.acts.containers.intro.0: [Deniz]: Ten times the users overnight. The servers are deep in the red.
story.acts.containers.intro.1: [Nova]: Containerize the app, scale it with Kubernetes. A pod can die and nobody should notice.
story.acts.containers.outro.0: [Nova]: The load is spread, the system heals itself. For the first time your phone didn't ring at night.
story.acts.containers.outro.1: [Deniz]: We're growing fast, but every deploy is a heart attack. And I'm done with 3 a.m. alarms.
story.acts.automation.title: ACT V — Sleeping Through the Night
story.acts.automation.intro.0: [Nova]: We're done releasing by hand. Pipeline: every push builds, tests and deploys itself.
story.acts.automation.intro.1: [Nova]: And we'll see inside the system — logs, metrics, alarms. Let's find the problem before the users do.
story.acts.automation.outro.0: [Nova]: The code tests and ships itself, and we catch problems early. The 3 a.m. alarms are nearly gone.
story.acts.automation.outro.1: [Deniz]: An audit is coming — security and cost review. Also, have you seen this AWS bill?
story.acts.mastery.title: ACT VI — The Architect
story.acts.mastery.intro.0: [Deniz]: Two problems: the risk of a security hole, and a bill that's out of control. You're closing both.
story.acts.mastery.intro.1: [Nova]: Final act. Tighten permissions, protect secrets, rein in the cost.
story.acts.mastery.outro.0: [Nova]: You did it. The system is secure, the cost is under control, and the team trusts you.
story.acts.mastery.outro.1: [Deniz]: You're Meridian's Platform Lead now. Six weeks ago the terminal scared you; today you're our backbone.
story.acts.mastery.outro.2: [Deniz]: We left Null alone and they burned out. We didn't leave you — we learned. Don't leave anyone alone either.
story.acts.mastery.outro.3: [Nova]: Go on, raise your own rookies now. 🚀
story.beats.c1q3.title: ◇ A TRACE
story.beats.c1q3.lines.0: [Nova]: That 'permission denied' — Null added that. The one engineer before you.
story.beats.c1q3.lines.1: [Nova]: They carried this place alone for months and left rushed patches like this. Every one of them is a time bomb.
story.beats.c3q1.title: ◇ A TRACE
story.beats.c3q1.lines.0: [Nova]: I saw it while poking at IAM: Null left an identity called 'app-bot' with full admin rights.
story.beats.c3q1.lines.1: [Nova]: Not now, but we're cleaning that bot up. Noted.
story.beats.c5q3.lines.0: [Deniz]: Let me be honest — these midnight crashes have been going on since Null left.
story.beats.c5q3.lines.1: [Deniz]: We keep patching their patches. We need someone to break the cycle. I hope that's you.
story.beats.c7q1.title: ◇ ROOT CAUSE
story.beats.c7q1.lines.0: [Nova]: Every trail leads to one place: a cron Null set up by hand has been locking the DB every night.
story.beats.c7q1.lines.1: [Nova]: It was never random. One fragile shortcut cost us months of sleep — and now it's visible.
story.beats.c8q1.title: ◇ THE LAST SHORTCUT
story.beats.c8q1.lines.0: [Nova]: That full-admin bot you just tore out — it was Null's last shortcut.
story.beats.c8q1.lines.1: [Nova]: Not a single time bomb they left is still ticking. For the first time the system is truly yours.
quests.c1q1.title: Cold Boot
quests.c1q1.brief.0: [Nova]: Alright, first assignment. Let's learn to find your way around this prod box —
quests.c1q1.brief.1: no panic, I'll tell you exactly what to type, one step at a time.
quests.c1q1.objectives.0.task: Find out where you are (print the working directory).
quests.c1q1.objectives.0.teach: Everything starts with 'where am I?'. pwd = print working directory.
quests.c1q1.objectives.1.task: List the files in this directory.
quests.c1q1.objectives.1.teach: ls shows the files/folders in a directory (dir on Windows).
quests.c1q1.objectives.2.teach: cat <file> = print the file's contents. First thing on a new server: read the notes.
quests.c1q1.objectives.2.success: README: 'Workspace is a mess — tidy the files first, then deploy.'
quests.c1q1.objectives.3.teach: cd = change directory. This is how you move between folders.
quests.c1q1.objectives.3.success: You're inside logs/. We'll dig through it shortly.
quests.c1q1.complete.0: [Nova]: You can navigate a terminal now. Let's clean up those scattered files.
quests.c1q2.title: The File Matrix
quests.c1q2.brief.0: [Nova]: We need a tidy folder for the deploy. Time to learn to manage the filesystem:
quests.c1q2.brief.1: create, copy, move, delete. This is an engineer's daily bread.
quests.c1q2.objectives.0.task: Go back up one level (to your home directory).
quests.c1q2.objectives.0.teach: .. = one folder up, ~ = your home directory. That's half of navigation right there.
quests.c1q2.objectives.1.task: Create a new folder called release.
quests.c1q2.objectives.1.teach: mkdir <name> = make directory. A tidy place for the files you'll ship.
quests.c1q2.objectives.2.task: Copy (or move) a file into the release folder.
quests.c1q2.objectives.3.teach: rm <file> = delete. CAREFUL: Linux has no recycle bin — it's permanent!
quests.c1q2.objectives.3.success: Temp file gone. Everything's in order.
quests.c1q2.complete.0: [Nova]: You own the filesystem. Next up: hunting down why the deploy keeps blowing up, in the logs.
quests.c1q3.title: Trail Tracker
quests.c1q3.brief.0: [Nova]: The deploy keeps failing and the reason is buried in the logs.
quests.c1q3.brief.1: Let's learn to pull the right clue out of thousands of lines: text processing.
quests.c1q3.objectives.0.task: Look at the last lines of the log file.
quests.c1q3.objectives.0.teach: tail <file> = shows the end of a file; tail -f streams it live. New errors land at the end.
quests.c1q3.objectives.0.success: The last lines are far too noisy — we need to filter.
quests.c1q3.objectives.1.task: Filter the log lines that contain 'error'.
quests.c1q3.objectives.1.teach: grep <pattern> <file> = keeps only the lines matching the pattern. The heart of reading logs.
quests.c1q3.objectives.2.task: Find where the deploy.sh file lives.
quests.c1q3.objectives.2.teach: find <where> -name <name> = searches the filesystem. Use it when you don't know where something is.
quests.c1q3.objectives.3.task: Count how many times the error repeated.
quests.c1q3.objectives.3.teach: wc -l counts lines; grep -c counts matches. Measuring the size of a problem matters.
quests.c1q3.objectives.3.success: 12 times! The root cause is clear: a permission problem. The next quest fixes it.
quests.c1q3.complete.0: [Nova]: You processed the text and got down to the root cause. That's what an engineer does most often.
quests.c1q4.title: Access Denied
quests.c1q4.brief.0: [Nova]: We've got our culprit: deploy.sh can't be executed — 'permission denied'.
quests.c1q4.brief.1: Time to learn Linux permissions: read / write / execute (rwx).
quests.c1q4.objectives.0.task: List the files with their permissions in detail.
quests.c1q4.objectives.0.teach: ls -l shows each file's permissions: rwx = read/write/execute.
quests.c1q4.objectives.0.success: The deploy.sh row is missing the x (execute) bit: -rw-r--r--
quests.c1q4.objectives.1.teach: chmod +x <file> = adds the execute bit. chmod = change mode.
quests.c1q4.objectives.2.teach: ./script runs a script in the directory you're standing in.
quests.c1q4.complete.0: [Nova]: Permissions are the foundation of security in the cloud. Nice work.
quests.c1q5.title: Ghost Process
quests.c1q5.brief.0: [Nova]: After the deploy the server is pinned at 100% CPU. Some process is running away.
quests.c1q5.brief.1: Read the machine's state, find the culprit and stop it.
quests.c1q5.objectives.0.teach: ps aux = lists every process with its user/CPU/memory; top shows it live.
quests.c1q5.objectives.0.success: PID 4711  node  99% CPU — there's your runaway.
quests.c1q5.objectives.1.teach: kill <PID> stops a process. If it resists, kill -9 <PID> forces it (process signals).
quests.c1q5.objectives.1.success: Process terminated. CPU is back to normal.
quests.c1q5.objectives.2.task: Check how full the disk is.
quests.c1q5.objectives.2.teach: df -h = shows free/used disk space in human-readable units (server review).
quests.c1q5.objectives.2.success: Disk is 64% full. No problem. The system is healthy.
quests.c1q5.complete.0: [Nova]: Being able to diagnose a system is what makes you a real engineer.
quests.c1q6.title: Daemon Awakening
quests.c1q6.brief.0: [Nova]: The server is missing a monitoring tool and a web service.
quests.c1q6.brief.1: Install a package, start a service, set an environment variable — the basics of bringing a server up.
quests.c1q6.objectives.0.teach: apt install (Debian/Ubuntu) or yum/dnf install (RHEL) = installs a package.
quests.c1q6.objectives.1.teach: systemctl start <service> = starts a service; enable makes it start at boot.
quests.c1q6.objectives.2.teach: systemctl status <service> = shows whether it's running and what the logs say.
quests.c1q6.objectives.3.teach: export NAME=value = defines an environment variable. This is how apps read their config (env/PATH).
quests.c1q6.objectives.3.success: APP_ENV=prod is set. The app switched to the right mode. Ch1 done! 🎉
quests.c1q6.complete.0: [Nova]: Packages, services and environment — you've finished the Linux fundamentals. Networking and Git are next.
quests.c2q1.title: The Lost Packet
quests.c2q1.brief.1: Let's diagnose the network layer by layer: reachability → name resolution → service.
quests.c2q1.objectives.0.task: Ping the server to see whether packets get through.
quests.c2q1.objectives.0.teach: ping <host> = the basic reachability test (the ICMP protocol).
quests.c2q1.objectives.0.success: We get a reply, but the name doesn't seem to resolve... DNS?
quests.c2q1.objectives.1.teach: dig / nslookup = shows which IP DNS maps the host to (DNS resolution).
quests.c2q1.objectives.1.success: DNS returns the right IP. So is the service answering?
quests.c2q1.objectives.2.task: Send a request to the HTTP service with curl.
quests.c2q1.objectives.2.teach: curl <URL> = an HTTP request from the command line. The bread and butter of testing an API.
quests.c2q1.objectives.2.success: 200 OK! Turns out a security group was blocking 443. Solved.
quests.c2q1.complete.0: [Nova]: Chasing network problems layer by layer is a superpower.
quests.c2q2.title: Layer 7
quests.c2q2.brief.0: [Nova]: The connection is still odd. Let's trace the packet's route, look at the ports,
quests.c2q2.brief.1: then connect to the server remotely and ship a file. (TCP/IP, routing, SSH)
quests.c2q2.objectives.0.task: Trace the packet's route to the server.
quests.c2q2.objectives.0.teach: traceroute <host> = shows every stop (hop) the packet passes through. It finds where things stall.
quests.c2q2.objectives.0.success: There's latency at hop 5 — the network path is visible now.
quests.c2q2.objectives.1.task: List the open ports / listening services.
quests.c2q2.objectives.1.teach: ss -tulpn (or netstat) = shows which port is being listened on by which service.
quests.c2q2.objectives.1.success: The service is listening on :8080. The port is open.
quests.c2q2.objectives.2.task: Connect to the server over SSH.
quests.c2q2.objectives.2.teach: ssh user@host = a secure connection to a remote server. This is daily life in the cloud.
quests.c2q2.objectives.2.success: You're on the server. Remote management is live.
quests.c2q2.objectives.3.task: Send a config file to the server.
quests.c2q2.objectives.3.teach: scp <local> user@host:<path> = copies files securely over SSH.
quests.c2q2.objectives.3.success: config delivered. The connectivity issue is fully resolved.
quests.c2q2.complete.0: [Nova]: You unpicked the network layer by layer and took command of a remote server. Now let's version the code.
quests.c2q3.title: The Branch Point
quests.c2q3.brief.0: [Nova]: You need to share your changes with the team. Git time.
quests.c2q3.brief.1: The classic flow: clone → branch → change → commit → push → PR.
quests.c2q3.objectives.0.teach: git clone <URL> = pulls a remote repo down to your machine.
quests.c2q3.objectives.1.teach: git checkout -b <name> or git switch -c <name> = create a new branch + switch to it.
quests.c2q3.objectives.2.teach: git add . then git commit -m 'message' = takes a snapshot.
quests.c2q3.objectives.3.task: Push the branch to the remote.
quests.c2q3.objectives.3.teach: git push = sends your commits to the remote repo. Then you open a PR.
quests.c2q3.objectives.3.success: Pushed. Ready to open a PR!
quests.c2q3.complete.0: [Nova]: Now you can work with a team safely. Version control = a time machine.
quests.c2q4.title: Chronos
quests.c2q4.brief.0: [Nova]: Sharing code isn't enough; you also need to read history, stay current and merge.
quests.c2q4.brief.1: Let's learn Git's 'time machine' side — the Fundamentals finale.
quests.c2q4.objectives.0.task: Check the state of your working tree.
quests.c2q4.objectives.0.teach: git status = shows what changed and what's staged for commit.
quests.c2q4.objectives.0.success: 2 modified, 1 new file. The picture is clear.
quests.c2q4.objectives.1.task: Review your changes line by line.
quests.c2q4.objectives.1.teach: git diff = shows the lines that changed since the last commit.
quests.c2q4.objectives.1.success: You've seen the changes — no surprises in this commit.
quests.c2q4.objectives.2.teach: git log --oneline = lists past commits in summary. Who did what, and when.
quests.c2q4.objectives.2.success: The recent commits are on screen. That's the time machine.
quests.c2q4.objectives.3.teach: git pull = fetches new commits from the remote and merges them in.
quests.c2q4.objectives.3.success: The team's changes are in. You're up to date.
quests.c2q4.objectives.4.task: Merge a branch into the current one.
quests.c2q4.objectives.4.teach: git merge <branch> = brings another branch's changes together with yours.
quests.c2q4.complete.0: [Nova]: You've got version control down too. Terminal, networking and Git — your foundation is solid now.
quests.c3q1.title: The Identity Matrix
quests.c3q1.brief.0: [Nova]: We're entering the real cloud! But identity comes first. The rule of the cloud: WHO before WHAT.
quests.c3q1.brief.1: In AWS everything starts with IAM — users, policies, roles. Less privilege = less risk.
quests.c3q1.objectives.0.teach: aws configure = sets your access key, secret and region. The door to everything.
quests.c3q1.objectives.1.task: Create an IAM user with limited privileges for the app.
quests.c3q1.objectives.1.teach: An IAM user = an identity. Never use the root account for day-to-day work.
quests.c3q1.objectives.2.task: Grant the user ONLY the permission it needs (a policy).
quests.c3q1.objectives.2.teach: A policy = a permission document. Least privilege: the least access possible, the least risk.
quests.c3q1.objectives.2.success: Read-only S3 access granted. Nothing more.
quests.c3q1.objectives.3.task: Create a role so services can reach each other securely.
quests.c3q1.objectives.3.teach: A role = lending an identity. EC2 reaches S3 through a role instead of storing keys.
quests.c3q1.objectives.3.success: Role ready. Servers will now get access without carrying keys.
quests.c3q1.complete.0: [Nova]: You've set up identity and access — the foundation of cloud security. Now let's weave the network.
quests.c3q2.title: The Virtual Backbone
quests.c3q2.brief.0: [Nova]: Let's build the private network our servers will live in: a VPC.
quests.c3q2.brief.1: CIDR for the IP range, subnets to divide it, a gateway for the internet, a security group for the wall.
quests.c3q2.objectives.0.task: Create a VPC in the 10.0.0.0/16 range.
quests.c3q2.objectives.0.teach: A VPC = your own isolated network. The CIDR block sets its IP range (10.0.0.0/16 ≈ 65k addresses).
quests.c3q2.objectives.1.task: Create a public subnet inside the VPC.
quests.c3q2.objectives.1.teach: A subnet = a slice of the VPC. A public subnet faces the internet; a private one doesn't.
quests.c3q2.objectives.2.teach: An Internet Gateway = connects the VPC to the internet. Without it you can't get out.
quests.c3q2.objectives.2.success: IGW created. The network can face outward.
quests.c3q2.objectives.3.task: Create a security group (firewall) to control the traffic.
quests.c3q2.objectives.3.teach: A security group = a firewall at the instance level. You decide which port is open to whom.
quests.c3q2.objectives.3.success: web-sg ready. The network layer is done.
quests.c3q2.complete.0: [Nova]: You built your own cloud network from scratch. The VPC is the backbone of cloud engineering.
quests.c3q3.title: Machine Awakening
quests.c3q3.brief.0: [Nova]: The network is ready; now let's put a server inside it: EC2.
quests.c3q3.brief.1: A key pair, an instance type, launch it, then an Elastic IP for a fixed address.
quests.c3q3.objectives.0.task: Create a key pair for SSH access to the server.
quests.c3q3.objectives.0.teach: A key pair = your SSH key. Keep the private key safe; you connect with it instead of a password.
quests.c3q3.objectives.0.success: cq-key created. Save the private key.
quests.c3q3.objectives.1.task: Launch a t3.micro EC2 instance (Free Tier).
quests.c3q3.objectives.1.teach: The instance type = the CPU/RAM size. t3.micro is Free Tier eligible.
quests.c3q3.objectives.2.teach: describe-instances = shows the state and IP. It should say 'running'.
quests.c3q3.objectives.2.success: i-0abc123 running. The server is up.
quests.c3q3.objectives.3.task: Allocate a fixed public IP (an Elastic IP).
quests.c3q3.objectives.3.teach: An Elastic IP = a fixed public IP that survives a server restart.
quests.c3q3.objectives.3.success: Elastic IP allocated. The address is stable now.
quests.c3q3.complete.0: [Nova]: You brought your first server up inside your own network. Compute is yours.
quests.c3q4.title: The Object Vault
quests.c3q4.brief.0: [Nova]: Let's put the app's files into durable storage: S3.
quests.c3q4.brief.1: Create a bucket, upload, then turn on versioning to guard against accidental deletes.
quests.c3q4.objectives.0.teach: aws s3 mb s3://<name> = 'make bucket'. Names must be globally unique.
quests.c3q4.objectives.1.task: Upload a file to the bucket.
quests.c3q4.objectives.1.success: File uploaded. The static site is live!
quests.c3q4.objectives.2.task: Enable versioning on the bucket (accidental-delete protection).
quests.c3q4.objectives.2.teach: Versioning = keeps every version; delete the wrong thing and you can roll it back. Storage classes (Standard/IA/Glacier) tune the cost.
quests.c3q4.objectives.2.success: Versioning on. Deletes are reversible now.
quests.c3q4.complete.0: [Nova]: You've got object storage: scalable, cheap, durable.
quests.c3q5.title: The Data Core
quests.c3q5.brief.0: [Nova]: The app needs data. Don't run the database yourself — let AWS run it: RDS.
quests.c3q5.brief.1: Create it, watch its state, stop it when unused (cost!). Free Tier: db.t3.micro.
quests.c3q5.objectives.0.task: Create a db.t3.micro MySQL RDS instance.
quests.c3q5.objectives.0.teach: RDS = a managed database. Backups, patching and replication are AWS's job; you just use it.
quests.c3q5.objectives.1.teach: describe-db-instances = once it says 'available', it's ready for connections.
quests.c3q5.objectives.2.task: Stop the database you aren't using (Free Tier / cost).
quests.c3q5.objectives.2.teach: An idle DB burns money. Stop it when you're not using it — an engineer's cost reflex.
quests.c3q5.objectives.2.success: cq-db stopped. The bill is under control. Cloud Core done! 🎉
quests.c3q5.complete.0: [Nova]: IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS — you can stand an application up on AWS end to end now.
quests.c4q1.title: Genesis
quests.c4q1.brief.0: [Nova]: Clicking by hand is error-prone and impossible to repeat. Put the infrastructure IN CODE — Terraform.
quests.c4q1.brief.1: The core loop: init → format → validate → preview → apply. The same result, every time.
quests.c4q1.objectives.0.teach: terraform init = downloads providers and modules and prepares the directory. The first command in any project.
quests.c4q1.objectives.0.success: Terraform initialized. The AWS provider was downloaded.
quests.c4q1.objectives.1.task: Put the code into standard formatting.
quests.c4q1.objectives.1.teach: terraform fmt = auto-aligns your HCL files. Keeps a team consistent.
quests.c4q1.objectives.2.task: Validate that the code is well-formed.
quests.c4q1.objectives.2.teach: terraform validate = checks syntax and consistency (without applying).
quests.c4q1.objectives.3.teach: terraform plan = shows what would change WITHOUT applying it. Always plan first.
quests.c4q1.objectives.3.success: Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
quests.c4q1.objectives.4.teach: terraform apply = turns the plan into reality.
quests.c4q1.objectives.4.success: Apply complete! 3 resources created — no clicking, fully reproducible.
quests.c4q1.complete.0: [Nova]: You've set up the IaC loop. From here on, infrastructure = code = reliability.
quests.c4q2.title: The Parametric System
quests.c4q2.brief.0: [Nova]: Hard-coded values are bad. Flex the code with variables, share the results with outputs.
quests.c4q2.objectives.0.task: Run a plan with an input variable.
quests.c4q2.objectives.0.teach: An input variable = a parameter of your code. You pass a value from outside with -var.
quests.c4q2.objectives.0.success: 3 instances planned. The code is flexible now.
quests.c4q2.objectives.1.task: Apply using an environment-specific variable file.
quests.c4q2.objectives.1.teach: Files like prod.tfvars carry per-environment values (-var-file).
quests.c4q2.objectives.2.teach: output = the values your infrastructure hands back. You read them with terraform output.
quests.c4q2.objectives.3.teach: terraform console = a REPL for trying out HCL expressions and variables.
quests.c4q2.complete.0: [Nova]: With variables and outputs your code is reusable now.
quests.c4q3.title: The State Map
quests.c4q3.brief.0: [Nova]: Terraform keeps reality in a 'state' file. Learn to read it and to repair it.
quests.c4q3.objectives.0.task: List the resources in the state.
quests.c4q3.objectives.0.teach: terraform state list = lists every resource Terraform manages.
quests.c4q3.objectives.1.teach: terraform state show <address> = shows every field of a single resource.
quests.c4q3.objectives.1.success: All of the web instance's attributes are on screen.
quests.c4q3.objectives.2.task: Bring a hand-created resource under Terraform.
quests.c4q3.objectives.2.teach: terraform import = adds an existing (manually created) resource to the state; it takes over management without recreating it.
quests.c4q3.objectives.2.success: The old bucket is under Terraform management now.
quests.c4q3.objectives.3.teach: terraform apply -replace=<address> = destroys and recreates a single resource (formerly: taint).
quests.c4q3.complete.0: [Nova]: Being able to read and repair state is the skill that saves you in the real world.
quests.c4q4.title: Modular Architecture
quests.c4q4.brief.0: [Nova]: Kill the repetition with modules, separate environments with workspaces, then clean up properly.
quests.c4q4.objectives.0.task: Download/update the modules used by the code.
quests.c4q4.objectives.0.teach: terraform get = downloads the modules referenced in your source. (init does it too; get is modules only.)
quests.c4q4.objectives.0.success: The vpc and ec2 modules were downloaded.
quests.c4q4.objectives.1.teach: A workspace = isolated state for the same code (dev/prod). terraform workspace new prod.
quests.c4q4.objectives.1.success: The prod workspace was created and selected.
quests.c4q4.objectives.2.teach: terraform graph = emits the resources' dependency graph (DOT). You see what depends on what.
quests.c4q4.objectives.3.task: Tear everything down with one command (cost!).
quests.c4q4.objectives.3.teach: terraform destroy = deletes everything it created. Cleaning up after a test = cost control.
quests.c4q4.objectives.3.success: Destroy complete! Resources deleted. The IaC module is done! 🎉
quests.c4q4.complete.0: [Nova]: Modules, workspaces and a clean lifecycle — you code infrastructure like a professional now.
quests.c5q1.title: Container Genesis
quests.c5q1.brief.0: [Nova]: The 'works on my machine' era is over. Package it with Docker.
quests.c5q1.brief.1: The app plus its dependencies in a single image. It runs the same everywhere.
quests.c5q1.objectives.0.task: Build an image from the Dockerfile.
quests.c5q1.objectives.0.teach: docker build -t <name> . = reads the Dockerfile and produces an image.
quests.c5q1.objectives.1.task: Run a container from the image.
quests.c5q1.objectives.1.teach: docker run = brings the image to life. -p publishes a port.
quests.c5q1.objectives.2.teach: docker ps = shows the running containers.
quests.c5q1.objectives.3.task: Bring the whole stack up with compose.
quests.c5q1.objectives.3.teach: docker compose up = starts several services (app+db) with one command.
quests.c5q1.objectives.3.success: app + db are up together. Full stack in containers!
quests.c5q1.complete.0: [Nova]: You've laid Docker's foundation. Now make the data durable and share the image.
quests.c5q2.title: Persistent Memory
quests.c5q2.brief.0: [Nova]: Running the image isn't enough; get inside it, make the data durable, then push it to a registry.
quests.c5q2.brief.1: So other people can 'pull' your image — that's how a team works.
quests.c5q2.objectives.0.teach: docker exec -it <container> sh = runs a command/shell inside a running container. Perfect for debugging.
quests.c5q2.objectives.1.task: Create a volume for persistent data.
quests.c5q2.objectives.1.teach: A container's filesystem is ephemeral — delete it and the data is gone. A volume = durable storage.
quests.c5q2.objectives.1.success: The appdata volume is ready. The data outlives the container now.
quests.c5q2.objectives.2.task: Tag the image for the registry.
quests.c5q2.objectives.2.teach: docker tag <image> <registry/user/name:tag> = names it for a push to a registry.
quests.c5q2.objectives.3.task: Push the image to the registry.
quests.c5q2.objectives.3.teach: docker push = uploads the image to a registry like DockerHub/ECR; others fetch it with 'pull'.
quests.c5q2.objectives.3.success: Push complete. The image is reachable from anywhere now.
quests.c5q2.complete.0: [Nova]: With persistence and a registry you've gone pro on Docker. Now for the orchestra: Kubernetes.
quests.c5q3.title: Orchestration
quests.c5q3.brief.0: [Nova]: One container isn't enough. Scale it and make it resilient with Kubernetes.
quests.c5q3.brief.1: kubectl = Kubernetes' command line. The concepts: pod, deployment, service.
quests.c5q3.objectives.0.task: List the nodes in the cluster.
quests.c5q3.objectives.0.teach: kubectl get nodes = shows the machines in the cluster.
quests.c5q3.objectives.1.teach: kubectl create deployment --image= = deploys the application.
quests.c5q3.objectives.2.teach: kubectl get pods = lists the pods that came up.
quests.c5q3.objectives.2.success: web-xxxx  1/1  Running. The app is up.
quests.c5q3.objectives.3.task: Expose the deployment with a Service.
quests.c5q3.objectives.3.teach: A Service = stable access to your pods plus load balancing. Pods come and go; the Service stays put.
quests.c5q3.objectives.3.success: service/web exposed. Traffic is being distributed now.
quests.c5q3.complete.0: [Nova]: With a Deployment and a Service you've published your app on the cluster.
quests.c5q4.title: The Scale Engine
quests.c5q4.brief.0: [Nova]: Publishing is the start. Now scale it, configure it, manage versions and debug it.
quests.c5q4.objectives.0.teach: kubectl scale = changes the replica count. Load spreads out, and the service survives a dead pod.
quests.c5q4.objectives.1.teach: A ConfigMap = configuration kept out of the code (env vars, settings). For sensitive values you use a Secret.
quests.c5q4.objectives.1.success: app-config created. Config is separated from the code.
quests.c5q4.objectives.2.teach: kubectl rollout = manages rolling updates and rollbacks. undo returns you to the last good version.
quests.c5q4.objectives.2.success: Rolled back to the previous version. No downtime.
quests.c5q4.objectives.3.task: Debug by looking at a pod's logs.
quests.c5q4.objectives.3.teach: kubectl logs <pod> = shows a pod's logs. describe shows you the events and the reason as well.
quests.c5q4.objectives.3.success: The logs are on screen. You got to the root cause. The Containers module is done! 🎉
quests.c5q4.complete.0: [Nova]: Scaling, config, releases and debugging — you can operate Kubernetes now.
quests.c6q1.title: The Autonomous Line
quests.c6q1.brief.0: [Nova]: Testing and deploying by hand on every push isn't sustainable.
quests.c6q1.brief.1: Build a pipeline with GitHub Actions: build → test → deploy, fully automatic.
quests.c6q1.objectives.0.task: Create the folder for workflow files.
quests.c6q1.objectives.0.teach: GitHub Actions runs the YAML files under .github/workflows/.
quests.c6q1.objectives.1.teach: The first step of CI is the build. If it doesn't compile it won't even be tested — fast feedback.
quests.c6q1.objectives.1.success: Build succeeded. The artifact is ready.
quests.c6q1.objectives.2.task: Run the tests locally (before putting them in the pipeline).
quests.c6q1.objectives.2.teach: Tests are the heart of CI. They have to pass locally first: npm test / pytest and so on.
quests.c6q1.objectives.3.task: Commit and push the workflow (let the pipeline fire).
quests.c6q1.objectives.3.teach: The push triggers the workflow. Build and test run automatically on GitHub's servers.
quests.c6q1.objectives.3.success: Actions triggered: build ✔ test ✔. A green pipeline!
quests.c6q1.complete.0: [Nova]: Your code builds and tests itself now. Next: safe automatic delivery (CD).
quests.c6q2.title: The Deploy Gate
quests.c6q2.brief.0: [Nova]: The tests are green but we're not done. Now for safe, automatic DELIVERY: secrets, triggers, monitoring, deploy.
quests.c6q2.brief.1: No more 'pushing to prod by hand'.
quests.c6q2.objectives.0.task: Add the deploy secrets to the repository secrets.
quests.c6q2.objectives.0.teach: NEVER write deploy keys into the code. Keep them in GitHub repo secrets; Actions reads them at runtime.
quests.c6q2.objectives.1.teach: Some jobs (like a deploy) you want to trigger by hand. gh workflow run does exactly that.
quests.c6q2.objectives.2.teach: gh run watch/list = follows the pipeline's state from your terminal. If it goes red, you step in.
quests.c6q2.objectives.2.success: Every step green. The deploy job has started.
quests.c6q2.objectives.3.task: Apply the new version to the cluster (the deploy step).
quests.c6q2.objectives.3.teach: The last step of CD: apply the new version to the environment. kubectl apply turns manifests into reality.
quests.c6q2.objectives.3.success: The new version is live. No hands, fully traceable.
quests.c6q2.complete.0: [Nova]: Every approved change now reaches production safely, automatically and traceably.
quests.c7q1.title: The Invisible Layer
quests.c7q1.brief.0: [Nova]: The alarm went off at 3 a.m. Someone reports 'it's slow' — but where?
quests.c7q1.brief.1: The 3 pillars of observability: logs, metrics, traces.
quests.c7q1.objectives.0.teach: tail -f = shows new lines as they're appended to the file, live.
quests.c7q1.objectives.0.success: The logs keep repeating 'DB timeout'. That's the clue.
quests.c7q1.objectives.1.teach: CPU/memory/request metrics point at the bottleneck. For example: kubectl top pods.
quests.c7q1.objectives.1.success: The DB pod is in the red on memory. It doesn't have enough resources.
quests.c7q1.objectives.2.task: Hit the health endpoint to confirm.
quests.c7q1.objectives.2.teach: A health endpoint is a quick pulse check. Automated alarms watch it.
quests.c7q1.objectives.2.success: {db: degraded} — root cause confirmed. An alarm is set up in Grafana.
quests.c7q1.complete.0: [Nova]: You can't manage what you can't measure. But checking by hand isn't enough — the system should tell you.
quests.c7q2.title: The Signal Network
quests.c7q2.brief.0: [Nova]: Observability isn't reading logs one by one. Query metrics, set alarms, follow distributed traces, watch a dashboard.
quests.c7q2.brief.1: The goal: catch the problem BEFORE the user does.
quests.c7q2.objectives.0.teach: Prometheus metrics are queried with PromQL (up, http_requests_total, latency...).
quests.c7q2.objectives.0.success: up{job="web"} = 1. The service is up and metrics are flowing.
quests.c7q2.objectives.1.teach: Alerting rules (high error rate, latency) get validated before they ship: promtool.
quests.c7q2.objectives.2.teach: Grafana visualizes metrics. port-forward connects you to the dashboard from your machine.
quests.c7q2.objectives.2.success: Grafana is on :3000. The latency graph is on screen.
quests.c7q2.objectives.3.teach: Distributed tracing (Jaeger/OpenTelemetry) shows a request's path across services; the slow part becomes obvious.
quests.c7q2.objectives.3.success: Trace: the latency is in the DB call (820ms). Root cause visible. The Automation module is done! 🎉
quests.c7q2.complete.0: [Nova]: Metrics, alarms, dashboards and traces — you can see the system's nervous system now.
quests.c8q1.title: The Access Shield
quests.c8q1.brief.0: [Nova]: The final act: security and cost — the two things that make an engineer senior.
quests.c8q1.brief.1: Access and secrets first. Least privilege, locked-up secrets, an auditable account.
quests.c8q1.objectives.0.teach: Excess privilege = risk. First see who can reach what (least privilege).
quests.c8q1.objectives.0.success: app-bot has AdministratorAccess — far too broad! It needs narrowing.
quests.c8q1.objectives.1.task: Remove the excess privilege (apply least privilege).
quests.c8q1.objectives.1.teach: detach-user-policy = strips an unnecessary permission. As much access as needed, not one bit more.
quests.c8q1.objectives.1.success: AdministratorAccess detached. app-bot can only reach what it needs now.
quests.c8q1.objectives.2.task: Store the secret in a secret manager instead of in code.
quests.c8q1.objectives.2.teach: NEVER write an API key into the repo. Keep it in a vault like Secrets Manager.
quests.c8q1.objectives.2.success: The secret is in the vault. No plaintext passwords left in the repo.
quests.c8q1.objectives.3.task: Turn on the audit log — make it visible who did what.
quests.c8q1.objectives.3.teach: CloudTrail records every API call. During an incident, 'who, when, what' comes from here.
quests.c8q1.objectives.3.success: The audit trail is on. Every move is recorded now.
quests.c8q1.complete.0: [Nova]: Access and secrets are safe. But the data itself may still be exposed — let's protect it.
quests.c8q2.title: The Encryption Layer
quests.c8q2.brief.0: [Nova]: The most common breach: a bucket accidentally left open to the world. Close the data off, encrypt it, scan your code.
quests.c8q2.objectives.0.task: Block public access on the S3 bucket.
quests.c8q2.objectives.0.teach: A public access block = stops the bucket being opened to the internet by accident. Default: blocked.
quests.c8q2.objectives.0.success: Public access blocked. The data isn't visible from outside anymore.
quests.c8q2.objectives.1.task: Encrypt the data at rest in the bucket.
quests.c8q2.objectives.1.teach: put-bucket-encryption = encrypts data on disk automatically (SSE). Even if it's stolen it can't be read.
quests.c8q2.objectives.1.success: Encryption active (AES256). Data at rest is safe.
quests.c8q2.objectives.2.teach: Trivy (images) / Checkov (IaC) = catch known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations before they ship.
quests.c8q2.objectives.2.success: Scan complete: 2 critical issues found and patched. Clean.
quests.c8q2.complete.0: [Nova]: The data is locked and encrypted, the code is scanned. One thing left: the bill.
quests.c8q3.title: The Budget Lock
quests.c8q3.brief.0: [Nova]: Growth is great, a surprise invoice isn't. See the cost, cap it, tag it, cut the waste.
quests.c8q3.brief.1: Do this and you're not a rookie anymore — you're Meridian's architect.
quests.c8q3.objectives.0.teach: Cost Explorer (ce) breaks spend down by service and by day. Check it regularly.
quests.c8q3.objectives.0.success: $842 this month. Up 60% from last month — this needs control.
quests.c8q3.objectives.1.task: Set up a budget that warns you when a threshold is crossed.
quests.c8q3.objectives.1.teach: Budgets = a spending threshold plus an alarm. You get an email/alert before the bill balloons.
quests.c8q3.objectives.1.success: A $1000 monthly budget with an 80% alarm is set. No surprises.
quests.c8q3.objectives.2.task: Tag the resources (which team/project is spending).
quests.c8q3.objectives.2.teach: Cost allocation tags = split the cost by team or project. The answer to 'where is this money going?'.
quests.c8q3.objectives.2.success: Resources tagged. Cost is visible per team now.
quests.c8q3.objectives.3.task: Stop the idle resource (cut the waste).
quests.c8q3.objectives.3.teach: An unused instance burns money. Shutting it down = instant savings.
quests.c8q3.objectives.3.success: The test server is stopped. The bill is trending down. 🎉
quests.c8q3.complete.0: [Nova]: Security and cost — you closed both. The journey is complete.
quests.c8q3.complete.1: Terminal, networking, AWS, IaC, containers, CI/CD, observability and security: all yours now.
quests.c8q3.complete.2: Next comes the real world: grow your portfolio on GitHub, get ready for the AWS SAA certification.
modules.net.title: Network Ops
modules.net.desc: network diagnosis games: port scanning, DNS/routing, packet capture, firewalls
quests.netq1.title: The Port Map
quests.netq1.brief.0: [Nova]: Welcome to the network dojo. Real faults, real commands.
quests.netq1.brief.1: A service is unreachable. First find out which ports are open and who's listening.
quests.netq1.objectives.0.task: Scan the open ports on the target machine.
quests.netq1.objectives.0.teach: nmap = scans which ports are open on a remote host. The first step of diagnosis.
quests.netq1.objectives.1.teach: ss -tulpn (or netstat) = which port is listened on by which process on this machine.
quests.netq1.objectives.1.success: The 'api' process is listening on 8080, nothing is listening on 443.
quests.netq1.objectives.2.task: Find which process is holding a given port.
quests.netq1.objectives.2.teach: lsof -i :PORT (or fuser) = shows the process using that port.
quests.netq1.objectives.2.success: PID 3120 / api. The process is up, just on the wrong port.
quests.netq1.objectives.3.teach: nc -zv host port = tries a TCP connection to the port (scan/verify). telnet works too.
quests.netq1.objectives.3.success: 80 is open, 443 refuses. The service is up on the wrong port.
quests.netq1.complete.0: [Nova]: You've mapped the ports. The problem is that nothing ever listens on 443 — note it and keep going.
quests.netq2.title: The DNS Labyrinth
quests.netq2.brief.0: [Nova]: Sometimes the problem isn't the machine but the name resolution, or the route.
quests.netq2.brief.1: Untangle the DNS chain and the path the packet takes.
quests.netq2.objectives.0.task: Trace DNS resolution from the root servers.
quests.netq2.objectives.0.teach: dig +trace = shows step by step how a domain resolves, starting at the root.
quests.netq2.objectives.0.success: The authoritative server returns the old IP — the record was never updated.
quests.netq2.objectives.1.task: Query a reverse DNS entry or a specific record type.
quests.netq2.objectives.1.teach: dig -x IP = reverse DNS; dig MX/NS/TXT name = a specific record type.
quests.netq2.objectives.1.success: The reverse record points at a different host. The confusion is confirmed.
quests.netq2.objectives.2.teach: ip route = shows which gateway packets leave through. A wrong route = unreachable.
quests.netq2.objectives.2.success: The gateway for 10.0.0.0/24 is wrong. There's the break.
quests.netq2.objectives.3.task: Follow the path and latency hop by hop.
quests.netq2.objectives.3.teach: mtr / traceroute = shows every stop the packet passes and the latency, live.
quests.netq2.objectives.3.success: Packets vanish at hop 3 — it'll clear once the route is fixed.
quests.netq2.complete.0: [Nova]: You solved name resolution and routing. The map of the network is in your head now.
quests.netq3.title: Packet Hunter
quests.netq3.brief.0: [Nova]: When the logs go quiet we look at the truth on the wire: the packets.
quests.netq3.brief.1: Capture the traffic, inspect the TLS handshake.
quests.netq3.objectives.0.teach: tcpdump -i <interface> <filter> = captures packets crossing the network. The filter is essential or you'll drown.
quests.netq3.objectives.0.success: SYN goes out but no SYN-ACK comes back — the other side is refusing.
quests.netq3.objectives.1.task: See the connection's details with curl (verbose).
quests.netq3.objectives.1.teach: curl -v = prints the DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP steps one by one. Where it breaks becomes obvious.
quests.netq3.objectives.1.success: It stalls at the TLS handshake: a certificate mismatch.
quests.netq3.objectives.2.teach: openssl s_client -connect host:443 = shows the certificate the server presents.
quests.netq3.objectives.2.success: The certificate belongs to the wrong domain, and it's expired. That's the root cause.
quests.netq3.objectives.3.teach: tshark -r file.pcap = reads/filters a saved capture (Wireshark's CLI).
quests.netq3.objectives.3.success: The analysis is clear: everything points at the certificate. It needs renewing.
quests.netq3.complete.0: [Nova]: You went down to the packet level. That skill is what makes people call you a wizard.
quests.netq4.title: Behind the Wall
quests.netq4.brief.0: [Nova]: The last diagnosis: is a wall cutting the traffic? Read the rules, test, fix, verify.
quests.netq4.objectives.0.teach: iptables -L / nft list ruleset / ufw status = shows the current firewall rules.
quests.netq4.objectives.0.success: There's a DROP rule for 443 — the wall was cutting the traffic.
quests.netq4.objectives.1.teach: nc -zv host port = confirms from outside whether the port is really open or closed.
quests.netq4.objectives.1.success: 443 times out — the wall is confirmed, the firewall is definitely the problem.
quests.netq4.objectives.2.task: Add a rule and open the port.
quests.netq4.objectives.2.teach: ufw allow / iptables -A = adds an allow rule. Open only the port you need, not all of them.
quests.netq4.objectives.3.teach: curl -I = fetches headers only; a quick way to see whether the service answers now.
quests.netq4.objectives.3.success: 200 OK! The network fault is resolved. The Network Ops lab is done! 🎉
quests.netq4.complete.0: [Nova]: Ports, DNS, packets and firewalls — a network engineer's diagnostic arsenal is yours now. 🛰️
modules.scripting.title: Scripting
modules.scripting.desc: automation with Bash: scripts, loops/conditions, log parsing, cron
quests.scrq1.title: The Script Core
quests.scrq1.brief.0: [Nova]: If you've done the same thing by hand twice, write the third one. Your first script: a backup.
quests.scrq1.brief.1: Run it, pass arguments, read the exit code, debug it.
quests.scrq1.objectives.0.teach: Running a script needs the execute bit: chmod +x. The first line, #!/bin/bash (the shebang), says which interpreter runs it.
quests.scrq1.objectives.1.task: Run the script with an argument.
quests.scrq1.objectives.1.teach: The words you pass become $1, $2...; $@ is all of them. That's how one script serves several environments.
quests.scrq1.objectives.2.task: Check the last command's exit code.
quests.scrq1.objectives.2.teach: Every command returns an exit code: 0 = success, anything else = failure. $? holds the last one. This is the foundation of automation.
quests.scrq1.objectives.3.task: Debug the script by tracing it line by line.
quests.scrq1.objectives.3.teach: bash -x script = prints each line as it runs. The answer to 'why didn't it work?' lives here.
quests.scrq1.objectives.3.success: The trace is streaming; you can see what happened on which line.
quests.scrq1.complete.0: [Nova]: Your first script runs. Arguments and exit codes — the bricks of automation.
quests.scrq2.title: The Logic Circuit
quests.scrq2.brief.0: [Nova]: What makes a script smart: variables, loops, conditions. Let's dump the repetition on the machine.
quests.scrq2.objectives.0.teach: You assign with name=value and read with $name. It expands inside double quotes: "$name".
quests.scrq2.objectives.1.task: Walk every log file with a loop.
quests.scrq2.objectives.1.teach: for x in LIST; do ...; done = repeats for each item. The backbone of batch work.
quests.scrq2.objectives.1.success: app.log, db.log, web.log — all in one loop.
quests.scrq2.objectives.2.task: Use a condition to check whether a file exists.
quests.scrq2.objectives.2.teach: if [ CONDITION ]; then ...; fi. -f tests for a file, -d for a directory, -z for emptiness.
quests.scrq2.objectives.2.success: app.pid exists — the service is running.
quests.scrq2.objectives.3.task: Read a file line by line.
quests.scrq2.objectives.3.teach: while read line; do ...; done < file = processes a file line by line. The classic of log processing.
quests.scrq2.objectives.3.success: The lines were processed one by one.
quests.scrq2.complete.0: [Nova]: Variables, loops, conditions — your script can think now.
quests.scrq3.title: Text Mining
quests.scrq3.brief.0: [Nova]: Logs are a gold mine, but raw ore. Process them with the grep/awk/sed trio and pull meaning out.
quests.scrq3.objectives.0.teach: grep <pattern> <file> = keeps the lines containing the pattern. -i makes it case-insensitive.
quests.scrq3.objectives.1.teach: awk '{print $N}' = prints field N. The way to pull an IP/status/duration out of space-separated logs.
quests.scrq3.objectives.1.success: The first column (the IPs) was extracted.
quests.scrq3.objectives.2.task: Make a bulk change in the text.
quests.scrq3.objectives.2.teach: sed 's/old/new/g' = rewrites text in a stream. The tool for cleaning and normalizing logs.
quests.scrq3.objectives.3.task: Find the most frequent entry (count + sort).
quests.scrq3.objectives.3.teach: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn = counts duplicates and sorts them most-first. It answers 'which IP is hitting us hardest?'.
quests.scrq3.complete.0: [Nova]: The grep-awk-sed trio — an engineer's Swiss army knife. You've mastered it.
quests.scrq4.title: The Scheduler
quests.scrq4.brief.0: [Nova]: The last step: make the script run while you sleep. cron plus writing scripts that hold up.
quests.scrq4.objectives.0.teach: crontab -l = shows the current scheduled jobs. You edit them with -e.
quests.scrq4.objectives.0.success: No jobs yet. Let's add one.
quests.scrq4.objectives.1.task: Open the editor to add a new cron job.
quests.scrq4.objectives.1.teach: crontab -e. The format: min hour day month weekday command. E.g. '0 3 * * * /opt/backup.sh' = every day at 03:00.
quests.scrq4.objectives.1.success: The backup now runs automatically at 03:00 every night.
quests.scrq4.objectives.2.task: Check the script for syntax errors without running it.
quests.scrq4.objectives.2.teach: bash -n script = checks only the syntax, without executing. Essential before you ship to prod.
quests.scrq4.objectives.3.teach: set -euo pipefail = stop on error, stop on an undefined variable, don't swallow a pipe failure. The first line of a professional script.
quests.scrq4.objectives.3.success: The script no longer swallows errors silently. The Scripting lab is done! 🎉
quests.scrq4.complete.0: [Nova]: You wrote it, processed with it, scheduled it and hardened it. The machines work for you now. 📜
modules.docker.title: Docker Deep Dive
modules.docker.desc: image layers, volumes/networks, registries, mastering compose
quests.dkq1.title: The Image Factory
quests.dkq1.brief.0: [Nova]: You know the basic build. Now learn to make an image SMALL and FAST — layers and multi-stage.
quests.dkq1.objectives.0.teach: docker build -t name:tag . = reads the Dockerfile layer by layer and produces an image. Each line is a layer = cache.
quests.dkq1.objectives.1.teach: docker history = shows each layer's size and command. This is how you find the bloated one.
quests.dkq1.objectives.1.success: Biggest layer: apt install (280MB). Target acquired.
quests.dkq1.objectives.2.teach: docker images = shows local images and their sizes. A small image = a fast deploy and a smaller attack surface.
quests.dkq1.objectives.2.success: app:1.0 → 412MB. We're going to bring that down.
quests.dkq1.objectives.3.task: Take only what you need with a multi-stage build.
quests.dkq1.objectives.3.teach: --target builds a specific stage from the Dockerfile. You drop the build tools and carry only the runnable artifact.
quests.dkq1.complete.0: [Nova]: From 412MB to 74MB. You've got layers and multi-stage — the image is elegant now.
quests.dkq2.title: The Persistent Link
quests.dkq2.brief.0: [Nova]: Containers are temporary. Durable data = a volume; containers talking to each other = a network.
quests.dkq2.objectives.0.task: Create a volume for persistent data.
quests.dkq2.objectives.0.teach: docker volume create = storage that outlives the container. DB data never belongs on a container's filesystem.
quests.dkq2.objectives.1.task: Run the container with the volume mounted.
quests.dkq2.objectives.1.teach: docker run -v volume:/path = mounts the volume inside the container. The data is independent of the container now.
quests.dkq2.objectives.1.success: MySQL's data lives in dbdata; it survives rebuilding the container.
quests.dkq2.objectives.2.task: Create a dedicated network for the containers.
quests.dkq2.objectives.2.teach: docker network create = an isolated network where containers reach each other by name.
quests.dkq2.objectives.3.task: Run the container attached to that network.
quests.dkq2.objectives.3.teach: docker run --network appnet = puts the container on the network; it can now reach others by a name like 'db'.
quests.dkq2.objectives.3.success: app reaches the database by the name 'db' now.
quests.dkq2.complete.0: [Nova]: Persistence and networking — you've wired the containers together like a real system.
quests.dkq3.title: The Registry Network
quests.dkq3.brief.0: [Nova]: An image nobody can pull is useless. Push it to a registry, then inspect it in depth.
quests.dkq3.objectives.0.task: Log in to a container registry.
quests.dkq3.objectives.0.teach: docker login = authenticates against a registry like DockerHub/GHCR/ECR. Required before a push.
quests.dkq3.objectives.1.task: Tag the image with the registry name.
quests.dkq3.objectives.1.teach: docker tag <local> <registry/user/name:tag> = the right name for a push.
quests.dkq3.objectives.2.task: Push the image to the registry.
quests.dkq3.objectives.2.teach: docker push = uploads the image to the registry; others pull it. It's the heart of CI/CD too.
quests.dkq3.objectives.2.success: Push complete. The image is reachable from anywhere.
quests.dkq3.objectives.3.teach: docker inspect = the full JSON detail: env, mounts, network, entrypoint... The last stop of debugging.
quests.dkq3.complete.0: [Nova]: Share and inspect — you can manage an image end to end.
quests.dkq4.title: Stack Command
quests.dkq4.brief.0: [Nova]: Manage a multi-service stack from one file, scale it, debug it — and leave the place tidy.
quests.dkq4.objectives.0.task: Bring the whole stack up with compose.
quests.dkq4.objectives.0.teach: docker compose up = starts every service in compose.yml (app+db+cache) with one command.
quests.dkq4.objectives.1.teach: --scale service=N = runs N copies of that service. Compose's way of spreading load.
quests.dkq4.objectives.1.success: The web service is at 3 copies. Traffic is spreading.
quests.dkq4.objectives.2.task: Debug by looking at a service's logs.
quests.dkq4.objectives.2.teach: docker logs / docker compose logs = shows a service's output. Your first diagnostic tool.
quests.dkq4.objectives.2.success: The logs are streaming; the problem is visible.
quests.dkq4.objectives.3.teach: docker system prune = deletes idle resources; it reclaims disk and reduces clutter. Do it regularly.
quests.dkq4.objectives.3.success: 3.2GB reclaimed. The Docker Deep Dive lab is done! 🎉
quests.dkq4.complete.0: [Nova]: Compose, scaling, debugging and cleanup — you're a Docker expert now. 🐳
modules.terraform.title: Terraform Pro
modules.terraform.desc: module design, remote state & locking, drift, CI-safe apply
quests.tfq1.title: The Module Blueprint
quests.tfq1.brief.0: [Nova]: Not copy-pasted HCL — reusable modules. That's the professional move.
quests.tfq1.objectives.0.task: Download/update the modules used by the code.
quests.tfq1.objectives.0.teach: terraform get -update = fetches and refreshes the modules (registry/git/local) referenced in your source.
quests.tfq1.objectives.0.success: The vpc, ec2 and rds modules were updated.
quests.tfq1.objectives.1.teach: terraform providers = shows which module depends on which provider and version.
quests.tfq1.objectives.1.success: 3 modules, a single aws provider (~> 5.0). Clean.
quests.tfq1.objectives.2.teach: terraform fmt -recursive = aligns every module file in the subdirectories.
quests.tfq1.objectives.3.task: Get the module output in a machine-readable format.
quests.tfq1.objectives.3.teach: terraform output -json = emits outputs as JSON; other tools and scripts can consume it.
quests.tfq1.complete.0: [Nova]: Modules = less repetition, far more consistency. Your infrastructure is Lego now.
quests.tfq2.title: The Remote State Lock
quests.tfq2.brief.0: [Nova]: State doesn't live on your laptop. You need shared, locked remote state — otherwise people collide.
quests.tfq2.objectives.0.task: Move/configure the state to a remote backend (S3+DynamoDB).
quests.tfq2.objectives.0.teach: terraform init -backend-config=... = moves the state to a shared backend like S3; DynamoDB provides the lock.
quests.tfq2.objectives.0.success: State moved to S3; the lock lives in DynamoDB. The team is safe.
quests.tfq2.objectives.1.task: Pull the remote state and inspect it.
quests.tfq2.objectives.1.teach: terraform state pull = downloads the remote state (JSON). You see exactly what's tracked.
quests.tfq2.objectives.2.teach: If an apply crashes the lock stays stuck. terraform force-unlock <ID> releases it safely.
quests.tfq2.objectives.2.success: Lock released; the team can apply again.
quests.tfq2.objectives.3.task: Rename a resource inside the state (refactor).
quests.tfq2.objectives.3.teach: terraform state mv old.address new.address = moves the resource in state without deleting it; the key to refactoring.
quests.tfq2.objectives.3.success: The address is updated; the resource was not recreated.
quests.tfq2.complete.0: [Nova]: Remote state and locking — the foundation of working safely with a team.
quests.tfq3.title: Drift Detection
quests.tfq3.brief.0: [Nova]: Someone made a change by hand in the console — 'drift'. Catch it, reconcile it, and intervene surgically when you must.
quests.tfq3.objectives.0.task: Detect the gap between the real world and the code (drift).
quests.tfq3.objectives.0.teach: terraform plan -refresh-only = compares resources to reality without applying anything. Manual changes surface.
quests.tfq3.objectives.0.success: Drift found: the security group was changed by hand.
quests.tfq3.objectives.1.teach: terraform apply -refresh-only = syncs the state to reality, not the code (it changes no resources).
quests.tfq3.objectives.2.task: Plan against a single targeted resource.
quests.tfq3.objectives.2.teach: terraform plan -target=ADDRESS = handles only that resource in a large estate. Use it carefully — it hides the bigger picture.
quests.tfq3.objectives.2.success: Only the security group was planned.
quests.tfq3.objectives.3.task: Show the current state in human-readable form.
quests.tfq3.objectives.3.teach: terraform show = dumps a saved plan or the current state in readable form.
quests.tfq3.objectives.3.success: The current state is on screen; the drift is closed.
quests.tfq3.complete.0: [Nova]: You spotted the drift and reconciled it. You're keeping the 'the code is the truth' discipline.
quests.tfq4.title: Autonomous Apply
quests.tfq4.brief.0: [Nova]: 'apply' in a pipeline must not be roulette. Save the plan, apply exactly that, put the gates in place.
quests.tfq4.objectives.0.task: Save the plan to a file (deterministic).
quests.tfq4.objectives.0.teach: terraform plan -out=tfplan = writes the plan to a file, so what gets applied is exactly what was approved.
quests.tfq4.objectives.1.teach: terraform apply tfplan = asks for no confirmation and applies exactly that plan. Ideal for CI.
quests.tfq4.objectives.1.success: The approved plan was applied as-is.
quests.tfq4.objectives.2.task: The format gate: enforce formatting in CI.
quests.tfq4.objectives.2.teach: terraform fmt -check = returns an error (exit != 0) if any file is unformatted. It blocks the merge in CI.
quests.tfq4.objectives.2.success: Every file is formatted. The gate is green.
quests.tfq4.objectives.3.teach: tfsec / checkov / tflint = catch vulnerabilities and misconfiguration in HCL before the merge.
quests.tfq4.objectives.3.success: 1 warning: a public S3 bucket. Fixed. The Terraform Pro lab is done! 🎉
quests.tfq4.complete.0: [Nova]: A deterministic plan plus format and security gates — you drive your infrastructure through CI with confidence. 🌍
modules.ansible.title: Ansible
modules.ansible.desc: configuration management with inventories, playbooks, roles and vault
quests.ansq1.title: Inventory Scan
quests.ansq1.brief.0: [Nova]: No more SSH-ing into 50 servers by hand. Ansible is agentless — SSH is all it needs.
quests.ansq1.brief.1: Get to know the inventory first: who's out there, are they reachable, what's running on them?
quests.ansq1.objectives.0.task: List every host in the inventory.
quests.ansq1.objectives.0.teach: ansible-inventory --list = dumps the hosts and groups from your inventory file as JSON. Verifying the inventory is always step one.
quests.ansq1.objectives.1.teach: ansible all -m ping = runs the 'ping' module against each host (not ICMP — an SSH+Python check).
quests.ansq1.objectives.2.task: Run an ad-hoc command against a group.
quests.ansq1.objectives.2.teach: ansible <group> -a "command" = a one-off command without writing a playbook. Perfect for quick diagnosis.
quests.ansq1.objectives.2.success: Uptime came back from all 4 web servers. One has been up for 200 days.
quests.ansq1.objectives.3.task: Gather system information (facts) from the hosts.
quests.ansq1.objectives.3.teach: The setup module = returns all of a host's 'facts': OS, IP, RAM and more. The basis for writing conditions in playbooks.
quests.ansq1.complete.0: [Nova]: You know the inventory. That's where Ansible's power starts: one command, fifty servers.
quests.ansq2.title: The Playbook Core
quests.ansq2.brief.0: [Nova]: An ad-hoc command is temporary. The playbook is what lasts: in YAML you say 'the system shall look like this'.
quests.ansq2.brief.1: But before it hits prod: check the syntax, dry-run it, then apply.
quests.ansq2.objectives.0.teach: --syntax-check = validates the YAML and task structure without running it. That's the first gate.
quests.ansq2.objectives.1.task: Dry-run it: see what would change.
quests.ansq2.objectives.1.teach: --check = reports what would change without changing anything. Like Terraform's 'plan'.
quests.ansq2.objectives.1.success: changed=7 (dry). nginx will be installed, the config updated.
quests.ansq2.objectives.2.task: Run it against a single group only.
quests.ansq2.objectives.2.teach: --limit <group> = applies the playbook only to the selected hosts. The way to do a staged (canary) rollout.
quests.ansq2.objectives.2.success: Only the web group was updated. The staged rollout has begun.
quests.ansq2.objectives.3.teach: Run it once the checks pass. The ok/changed/failed counts in the output summarize the result.
quests.ansq2.objectives.3.success: ok=12 changed=7 failed=0. The whole fleet is on the same configuration.
quests.ansq2.complete.0: [Nova]: Syntax → check → limit → apply. Those four steps save you from a midnight disaster.
quests.ansq3.title: Role Architecture
quests.ansq3.brief.0: [Nova]: One giant playbook becomes impossible to maintain. Split it into roles — the same logic as Terraform modules.
quests.ansq3.objectives.0.teach: ansible-galaxy init roles/<name> = creates tasks/, handlers/, templates/ and defaults/ in the standard layout.
quests.ansq3.objectives.0.success: The roles/nginx scaffold is ready (tasks, handlers, templates, defaults).
quests.ansq3.objectives.1.teach: It downloads the community-written roles listed in requirements.yml. Don't reinvent the wheel.
quests.ansq3.objectives.2.task: List the tasks the playbook will run.
quests.ansq3.objectives.2.teach: --list-tasks = shows which role runs which tasks, without executing. The way to understand a big playbook.
quests.ansq3.objectives.3.task: Run only the tasks with a given tag.
quests.ansq3.objectives.3.teach: --tags = runs only the relevant part of the playbook. The way to say 'just update the config'.
quests.ansq3.objectives.3.success: Only the nginx tasks ran (6 seconds).
quests.ansq3.complete.0: [Nova]: Roles and tags — your infrastructure code is readable and manageable piece by piece now.
quests.ansq4.title: The Vault Protocol
quests.ansq4.brief.0: [Nova]: Two last lessons: encrypt the secrets, then prove idempotency.
quests.ansq4.brief.1: Ansible's promise is this: run the same playbook 100 times and the system stays exactly the same.
quests.ansq4.objectives.0.teach: ansible-vault encrypt = encrypts passwords/keys with AES; you can commit the encrypted form.
quests.ansq4.objectives.0.success: Encryption successful. No plaintext passwords in the repo anymore.
quests.ansq4.objectives.1.task: View the encrypted file without decrypting it to disk.
quests.ansq4.objectives.1.teach: ansible-vault view = shows the file on screen without decrypting it to disk. edit lets you change it the same way.
quests.ansq4.objectives.1.success: The contents are on screen; the file stayed encrypted on disk.
quests.ansq4.objectives.2.task: Run the playbook with the vault password.
quests.ansq4.objectives.3.task: Run the same playbook again and look at the diff (idempotency).
quests.ansq4.objectives.3.teach: --diff = shows line by line what changed. A well-written playbook reports changed=0 on the second run.
quests.ansq4.objectives.3.success: changed=0 — the system is already in the desired state. That's idempotency! The Ansible lab is done! 🎉
quests.ansq4.complete.0: [Nova]: Encrypted secrets and changed=0. You genuinely understand configuration management now. ⚙️
modules.kubernetes.title: Kubernetes
modules.kubernetes.desc: namespaces & quotas, probes & autoscaling, secrets & storage, diagnosis & Helm
quests.k8sq1.title: The Isolated Zone
quests.k8sq1.brief.0: [Nova]: You know the basics (deployments, services). Now carve the cluster up like a real production environment.
quests.k8sq1.brief.1: A namespace = isolation. A quota = stops one team eating the whole cluster.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.0.task: Create a separate namespace for prod.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.0.teach: A namespace = a logical partition inside the cluster. dev/staging/prod coexist in one cluster without colliding.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.1.task: Put a resource quota on the namespace.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.1.teach: A ResourceQuota = caps the total CPU/RAM/pod count that namespace can use. It protects the neighbouring team.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.2.teach: Typing -n prod on every command gets old. set-context changes the default (and cuts the risk of deploying to the wrong environment).
quests.k8sq1.objectives.3.task: List every resource in the namespace.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.3.teach: kubectl get all -n <ns> = shows that zone's pods/services/deployments at a glance.
quests.k8sq1.objectives.3.success: The prod zone is ready and isolated.
quests.k8sq1.complete.0: [Nova]: You partitioned and capped the cluster. That's rule one of a multi-team environment.
quests.k8sq2.title: Pulse & Scale
quests.k8sq2.brief.0: [Nova]: Kubernetes heals things for you — but only if you tell it what 'healthy' means.
quests.k8sq2.brief.1: Read the probes, then scale so the load handles itself.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.0.teach: describe = shows liveness/readiness probe state, restart count and events. This is where you learn why a pod keeps restarting.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.0.success: Liveness OK, Readiness failed x3 — the app is slow to start.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.1.teach: autoscale = raises and lowers the replica count based on CPU. It's what lets you sleep through a traffic spike.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.2.teach: get hpa = shows current/target CPU and the replica count. This tells you whether scaling actually works.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.2.success: web  45%/70%  2/10 replicas. The system is breathing.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.3.teach: kubectl top = live CPU/memory usage per pod. You look at this when setting quotas and limits.
quests.k8sq2.objectives.3.success: The busiest pod is at 380m CPU / 512Mi. Within quota.
quests.k8sq2.complete.0: [Nova]: Health checks plus autoscaling = a system that runs itself.
quests.k8sq3.title: Vault & Storage
quests.k8sq3.brief.0: [Nova]: You've seen ConfigMaps. Now sensitive data (Secrets) and persistent storage (PVCs).
quests.k8sq3.brief.1: Pods die, data doesn't — we're going to guarantee that.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.0.task: Create a Secret for the database password.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.0.teach: A Secret = sensitive data (passwords, tokens). Unlike a ConfigMap it's stored base64-encoded and access is restricted via RBAC.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.1.task: List the secrets (without leaking the values).
quests.k8sq3.objectives.1.teach: get secrets = shows names and types, not values. Seeing a value takes a separate command and a separate permission.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.1.success: db-cred (Opaque, 1 data). The value isn't shown — that's the correct behaviour.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.2.teach: A PersistentVolumeClaim = a request saying 'give me 10Gi of disk'. The data survives the pod being deleted.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.3.task: Verify the storage claim was fulfilled.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.3.teach: get pvc = shows whether the claim is Bound or Pending. If it stays Pending, you have a StorageClass problem.
quests.k8sq3.objectives.3.success: db-data  Bound  10Gi  gp3. The data is durable now.
quests.k8sq3.complete.0: [Nova]: Secrets are protected and data persists. Stateful workloads are safe now.
quests.k8sq4.title: The Diagnostic Net
quests.k8sq4.brief.0: [Nova]: Final lesson: how you diagnose things when they break, and how you package all of it (Helm).
quests.k8sq4.objectives.0.task: Review the cluster events in chronological order.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.0.teach: events = the answer to 'why didn't this pod start?'. The real causes — OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff — live here.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.0.success: FailedScheduling: insufficient CPU. Root cause found.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.1.task: Get inside the running pod and check.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.1.teach: kubectl exec = runs a command inside the container. Did the config really mount, does DNS resolve — you look live.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.1.success: You're inside the container. Env and mounts verified.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.2.task: Forward the service to your local machine.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.2.teach: port-forward = binds a service inside the cluster to localhost. The quick way to test without setting up an Ingress.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.2.success: localhost:8080 → the web service in the cluster. Testable.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.3.task: Install the application as a Helm chart.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.3.teach: Helm = Kubernetes' package manager. One chart plus a values file instead of dozens of YAMLs; versioning and rollback come built in.
quests.k8sq4.objectives.3.success: Release myapp deployed. The Kubernetes lab is done! 🎉
quests.k8sq4.complete.0: [Nova]: You've got the diagnostic reflex and Helm. The cluster isn't a stranger anymore. ☸️
